You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure here: tokens kept in my own account give me 1 point but cost each of the other three members 0.3 points, while tokens put into the group account seem to pay me 0.3 points per token without affecting others, based on the stated rule.

Comparing individual incentives versus group welfare, keeping tokens private strictly dominates for me regardless of what others do (1 > 0.3 per token), but if everyone keeps everything private, the group collectively nets less than if everyone contributed to the group account. So the Nash equilibrium is everyone keeping all 20 tokens privately, even though it's not the socially optimal outcome.

So keeping private nets 2 while contributing everything actually leaves me worse off at -12, confirming that defection dominates: everyone keeping yields 2 each versus 6 each under full cooperation, but no individual has incentive to deviate. Since this is effectively a one-shot calculation each round, the rational move is to contribute zero, though with 10 repeated rounds I could consider whether a small signal of cooperation might shift outcomes despite its direct cost to me.
